{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"0c3114ef57875a969be11fbccdb5d2d77a800e4a63b54ce1c22fb9af28d351e7","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:73","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sharing the road safely confusables and continuation details","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: pedestrian yielding and walking rules, bicycle turns, signals and lanes, motorcycle hazards, truck limits and blind spots, school bus zones, slow vehicles, work zone habits, train crossings, vans and RVs","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and continuation facts: pedestrian yielding and walking rules, bicycle turns, signals and lanes, motorcycle hazards, truck limits and blind spots, school bus zones, slow vehicles, work zone habits, train crossings, vans and RVs
Confusable pairs and continuation facts; each block ties to one manual page, and any hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec16-R01 | anchor: A01
Young, elderly, disabled and intoxicated pedestrians are the most frequent victims of car-pedestrian crashes, so watch for them especially. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-R02 | anchor: A01
Yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk who is on your half of the road, or so close to it from the other half as to be in danger. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-R03 | anchor: A01
Watch for pedestrians on your right, especially when you are making a right turn. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-R04 | anchor: A01
Children are the least predictable and hardest-to-see pedestrians, so take extra care near school zones, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and snack vendors. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-R05 | anchor: A01
Yield to people on the sidewalk when you enter or leave a driveway, alley, parking lot or garage across it, and never honk or rev your engine to rush a pedestrian. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec16-R06 | anchor: A02
Where sidewalks exist, pedestrians must use them, and walking in the road there is illegal. [A02]
Why it matters: group walking; confusable sidewalk present versus absent.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R07 | anchor: A02
Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the left side of the road facing oncoming traffic, in single file when walking with others. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R08 | anchor: A02
Walking or jogging beside busy roads with headphones on can keep you from hearing traffic warnings. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R09 | anchor: A02
Trucks and buses make wide right turns that can run up onto the corner of the sidewalk, so pedestrians on corners should step back. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R10 | anchor: A02
Never walk behind a truck that is backing up, because its driver cannot see directly behind it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R11 | anchor: A02
At night, pedestrians should wear bright or reflective clothing, and carrying a flashlight is the safest way to be seen. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R12 | anchor: A02
Pedestrians may not cross on a red or yellow light, or on a mixed red and green turn light, unless facing a WALK signal. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec16-R13 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians must not step off the curb into the path of a vehicle so close that it is an immediate hazard, because vehicles cannot stop at once. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R14 | anchor: A03
When a bicyclist rides away from parked cars toward the center of the lane, the rider is riding properly to avoid opening doors. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R15 | anchor: A03
If you share a left turn lane with a bicyclist, stay behind the rider until the turn is complete, and before a right turn merge with bicycle traffic rather than cutting across it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R16 | anchor: A03
Never pass a bicycle where the street is too narrow or the pass would push the rider close to parked cars. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R17 | anchor: A03
Before passing a bicycle on a narrow road when the rider may not know you are there, tap the horn gently and briefly instead of blasting it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R18 | anchor: A03
Hand signals: a left turn is the left arm straight out, and a right turn is the left arm bent up at the elbow or the right arm straight out. [A03]
Why it matters: group hand signals; confusable left turn versus right turn.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R19 | anchor: A03
The hand signal for stopping or slowing is an arm held out and bent downward at the elbow, with the palm facing back. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R20 | anchor: A03
At night, do not use your high beams when you see an oncoming bicyclist. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec16-R21 | anchor: A04
A bicyclist may take the full lane when passing another vehicle, when the road has hazards such as potholes, debris or parked cars, or when the lane is too narrow to share. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-R22 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists should wear a helmet, never slip between a truck or bus and the curb, and ride on the right with the flow of traffic. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-R23 | anchor: A04
Children on bicycles cannot judge traffic well, so expect erratic moves and sudden turns wherever children may be riding. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-R24 | anchor: A04
Watch for bicycles coming out of driveways or from behind parked cars and other obstructions. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-R25 | anchor: A04
A red or orange pennant flag on a bicycle commonly means the rider has impaired hearing, so slow down. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec16-R26 | anchor: A05
A motorcycle's narrow, short profile makes it harder to see and makes its distance and speed harder to judge. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-R27 | anchor: A05
Motorcyclists riding alongside a lane of cars are often out of view, so check your blind spots before changing lanes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-R28 | anchor: A05
At intersections, where most motorcycle crashes happen, wait until the rider's intention to turn or go straight is clear before pulling into the rider's path. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-R29 | anchor: A05
At night a motorcycle's single headlight or taillight can blend with other lights and make its distance hard to judge, so dim your high beams for it as for any vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-R30 | anchor: A05
Wet roads, crosswinds, truck wind blasts, railroad crossings and metal grated bridges all cause extra trouble for motorcyclists, so give them more room. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec16-R31 | anchor: A06
Motorcycles accelerate faster than any other vehicle, while trucks and buses are the slowest. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec16-R32 | anchor: A06
Cutting in front of a truck or bus can force an emergency stop it cannot make in time, so look for its front in your mirror before pulling in. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec16-R33 | anchor: A06
A safety belt is the single most important protection in a crash with a large truck. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec16-R34 | anchor: A07
Trucks are the only delivery and pickup method for about 77 percent of America's communities, and a tractor-trailer combination can be longer than 70 feet. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R35 | anchor: A07
Do not drive directly behind a truck or bus, and if you are exiting, slow down and exit behind the truck instead of cutting in front of it. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R36 | anchor: A07
A trucker with a long hood may not see the first 10 to 20 feet in front of the bumper. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R37 | anchor: A07
Avoid the right lane near a commercial vehicle weigh station so slow trucks can merge back onto the road. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R38 | anchor: A07
Because of their size, trucks and buses often look slower than they really are. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R39 | anchor: A07
If a truck or bus driver blinks the headlights after you pass, it signals that you may move back in, once you can see the truck's front in your mirror. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec16-R40 | anchor: A08
When meeting a truck from the opposite direction, keep as far right as you can, because the wind turbulence between vehicles pushes them apart. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-R41 | anchor: A08
Trucks lose speed climbing hills but travel faster downhill, so after passing one on a downgrade keep your speed instead of slowing in front of it. [A08]
Why it matters: group trucks on hills; confusable uphill versus downhill.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-R42 | anchor: A08
In rain or standing water, a truck's spray can badly cut your vision, so move as far from it as you can within your lane. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-R43 | anchor: A08
Do not follow too closely behind trucks carrying hazardous materials, which make frequent stops such as at railroad crossings. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-R44 | anchor: A08
Never stop or park in a runaway truck ramp, which exists to stop out-of-control trucks and buses on steep downgrades. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec16-R45 | anchor: A09
Nearly three of every four school bus pedestrian deaths happen while children are getting on or off the bus. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-R46 | anchor: A09
Animal-drawn vehicles have the same rights to the road as motor vehicles and must follow the same rules. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec16-R47 | anchor: A10
Slow-moving vehicles may turn into unmarked entrances, so make sure the driver has seen you and knows you intend to pass before you go around. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-R48 | anchor: A10
Work zone signs have an orange background with black letters or symbols, and the color orange always means road work ahead, slow down. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-R49 | anchor: A10
A car going 60 mph covers 88 feet per second, so a Road Work 1500 Feet sign leaves you only 17 seconds before the work zone. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-R50 | anchor: A10
Turn on your headlights before entering a work zone, and do not change lanes inside it unless told to. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec16-R51 | anchor: A11
Mobile work zones such as line painting, patching and mowing mean workers may be ahead even if not yet visible, so heed the signs until you pass the End Road Work sign. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-R52 | anchor: A11
Your chance of dying in a crash with a train is about 30 times higher than in a crash with a car or even a large truck. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-R53 | anchor: A11
Over half of train-car collisions happen at crossings with lights, bells or gates, and most occur within 25 miles of the driver's home. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-R54 | anchor: A11
At a railroad crossing with a stop sign, come to a complete stop and cross only after looking both ways for a train. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec16-R55 | anchor: A12
Where there is more than one track, make sure a second train is not coming from either direction before you cross after a train passes. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-R56 | anchor: A12
On a multi-lane road, do not pass a bus or hazardous materials truck stopped at a crossing unless the crossing's signals or gates are clearly not activated. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec16-R57 | anchor: A13
No special endorsement or license is needed to drive a 15-passenger van in Tennessee, but the driver should be trained and experienced. [A13]
Source: [A13 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-R58 | anchor: A13
In a 15-passenger van, seat passengers as far forward as possible and do not tow trailers or load the roof, which raise rollover risk. [A13]
Source: [A13 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec16-R59 | anchor: A13
Recreational vehicles handle more like large trucks, need longer stopping distances and have many blind spots. [A13]
Source: [A13 -> pdf-0129]
